title: Probabilistic step controller for canary rollouts
creator: Asha Kapoor
description: Introduce a probabilistic step controller that adjusts canary traffic splits using online statistical confidence rather than purely time-based steps. The controller's goal is safer, faster rollouts by allowing adaptive increases when metrics show statistical improvement and halting or rolling back when guardrails indicate regression. This ticket covers design, implementation hooks in the rollout engine, integration tests, and a small pilot against low-risk models.
motivation: Current deterministic step schedules (e.g., 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 100%) are easy to reason about but either move too slowly for clear wins or too fast when the signal is noisy. A probabilistic controller can exploit high-confidence positive signals to accelerate rollouts and detect regressions earlier while preserving conservative defaults for noisy workloads.
proposal: Implement a controller that evaluates primary rollout metrics (latency P95, model error rate, hallucination score) over sliding windows and computes Bayesian credible intervals for performance delta vs baseline.
Make a decision rule: allow next step increase when lower bound of credible interval shows no regression beyond a configurable margin; otherwise hold or reduce traffic.
Support two modes: 'adaptive' (probabilistic, default for low-risk models) and 'deterministic' (legacy schedules for high-compliance customers).
Expose configuration: metric set, alpha (confidence), min-sample-size-per-step, max-step-size, cool-down window, shadow-traffic fraction for cross-checks.
Provide audit logs and explainability: human-readable decision summaries for each progression step and a link to the supporting metric windows.
Hook into auto-rollback: if regression exceeds rollback threshold for N consecutive windows, trigger automatic rollback to last known-good model with an incident alert.
Add canary simulation harness to the Console so PMs/SEs can preview rollout progress under synthetic traffic and metric distributions.
architecture_notes: Controller computes effect size and uncertainty using a Bayesian t-test (normal approximation on aggregated metrics) to produce a 90% credible interval for delta between canary and baseline.

Traffic split adjustments are probabilistic: server-side routing assigns each request a probability of routing to canary according to the controller's target; this maintains request-level independence and reduces correlation artifacts.

Use adaptive min-sample-size: require at least M requests and K completions (inference tokens) per variant before trusting the estimate; until then use a conservative growth schedule (e.g., +1% per hour).

Guardrails include hard SLO thresholds (latency P95 < target), error-rate ceilings, and qualitative signal from the quality monitor (evaluations on a small prompt set). Any breached guardrail forces an immediate hold or rollback depending on severity.

Implementation will live in rollout-controller-service with a lightweight policy DSL persisted in the rollout config. The runtime will call the controller every evaluation interval (configurable, default 5 minutes).
Fallback behavior: if metric ingestion fails or samples are insufficient, revert to deterministic step schedule and set 'data-missing' annotation on the rollout.
acceptance_criteria: Controller respects policy DSL and applies probabilistic increases in a canary experiment in dev environment.
Metrics dashboard displays decision rationale and underlying windows for each step in Console.
Auto-rollback triggers when defined regression conditions are met in end-to-end staging tests.
Simulation harness allows product team to run at least three synthetic scenarios and compare adaptive vs deterministic schedules.
Unit and integration tests cover edge cases: low traffic, bursty traffic, missing metrics, and metric lag.
Performance: controller evaluation adds <100ms median overhead to the control loop and scales to 200 concurrent rollouts per region.

risks: False positives: small but systematic measurement bias can cause premature rollout; mitigated by conservative defaults and focus on delta vs baseline rather than absolute numbers.
Complexity for operators: probabilistic decisions can be harder to interpret; mitigations are explanatory logs, simulation UI, and the ability to pin 'deterministic' mode per customer.
Metric latency: delayed signals could allow an unsafe increase; we add cool-down windows and require minimum sample sizes.
Performance overhead: frequent statistical computations could add CPU; we'll cache aggregated windows and precompute sufficient statistics.
Regulatory customers may require deterministic schedules — ensure a clear config flag to opt out.
testing_plan: Unit tests for Bayesian estimator and decision boundaries with synthetic distributions.
Stress tests: controller under 500 concurrent rollouts and simulated metric ingestion lag.
Canary e2e: run pilot with internal model A -> model B on staging traffic; assert expected behavior for three scenarios (clear improvement, noisy/no-signal, clear regression).
Chaos test: simulate missing metrics and verify fallback to deterministic schedule and operator alerting.
Manual review checklist for pilot: product sign-off, SRE sign-off, customer-facing docs drafted.
outcome_metrics: Time-to-full-rollout (median) for positive-signal experiments compared to deterministic baseline
Number of rollbacks avoided vs deterministic schedule (safety improvements)
Incidence of false-positive promotions (regressions that escaped guardrails)
Controller CPU and latency overhead per rollout lifecycle
Operator satisfaction score from pilot (qualitative feedback)
